answer_text: Chlorophyll in plant cells absorbs red and blue light for photosynthesis but reflects green light, which is why plants appear green to us.

Plant cells contain a pigment called chlorophyll, which plays a central role in photosynthesis. Chlorophyll strongly absorbs light in the red and blue wavelengths, which it uses to power the conversion of light energy into chemical energy. However, it does not absorb green wavelengths of light — instead it reflects them back, and that reflected green light is what we perceive when we look at a leaf.
Plants look green because chlorophyll reflects green light instead of absorbing it.

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane from a region of low solute concentration to a region of high solute concentration, until equilibrium is reached. A common example is a raisin swelling up when placed in water.

Osmosis refers to the passive diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Water moves from the side with lower solute concentration (higher water potential) to the side with higher solute concentration (lower water potential), continuing until the concentrations equalize on both sides. This is why plant root hair cells can absorb water from the soil, since the soil water has a lower solute concentration than the cell sap.

A stack follows LIFO (Last In First Out) order, meaning the most recently added element is the first one removed, like a stack of plates. A queue follows FIFO (First In First Out), where the first element added is the first one removed, like a line of people waiting.

A stack is a linear data structure where insertion and removal both happen at the same end, called the top. This gives it Last In First Out behavior — the last item pushed onto the stack is the first one popped off. A queue, in contrast, inserts elements at the rear and removes them from the front, giving it First In First Out behavior, so the earliest inserted element is the first one to be removed.
A stack only allows you to add and remove elements from one end, following LIFO order.
A stack and a queue are basically the same thing, just different names used in different programming languages.
